title: India's $133 Billion NRI Deposit Haul: How Much Was Fresh Money, and What Matures in 2029?
excerpt: Banks raised $132.98 billion in FCNR(B) deposits under the RBI's swap window — but much of it was leveraged money, not fresh savings. The deposits begin maturing in mid-2029, and Uday Kotak puts the eventual repayment bill at $160-170 billion with interest.
body:
• Banks mobilised $132.98 billion in FCNR(B) deposits under the RBI's special swap window by August 31; with overseas borrowings and ECBs, total inflows reached $143.6 billion.
  • Much of the haul was leveraged, not fresh savings: ICICI, which raised about $18 billion, said only about a quarter was plain NRI money, and GIFT City-backed loans funded close to half the system's total.
  • The deposits are 3-5 year money and start maturing in mid-2029; Uday Kotak estimates the repayment obligation, with interest, at $160-170 billion.
  • If you hold FCNR deposits from this window, your maturity choice matters at scale: in the 2013 window's 2016 unwind, about a quarter of the money stayed on — rollovers are what make 2029 orderly.

India's banks raised nearly $133 billion from non-resident Indians in under three months this year, roughly five times what the Reserve Bank of India's last such window managed in 2013. The headline suggests a vast vote of confidence by the diaspora. The composition of the money tells a more complicated story — and the bill comes due starting in 2029.

How the Window Worked

On June 8, the RBI unveiled a facility under which it would bear the full hedging cost for banks raising fresh three- to five-year FCNR(B) deposits — dollar term deposits that an NRI holds with an Indian bank and is repaid from in dollars. Normally the cost of hedging the rupee risk makes such deposits barely worth chasing. With the RBI absorbing that cost through a dollar-rupee swap, the money became cheaper than raising deposits at home: IDFC First put its all-in cost at about 6.8%, against roughly 7.8% for a comparable rupee deposit once reserve rules are counted, according to The Daily Brief by Zerodha. The RBI also waived cash-reserve and government-bond requirements on the deposits. The window, meant to reinforce India's external buffers amid pressure on the rupee, closed on August 31, a month ahead of schedule — and nearly half the money arrived in the last ten days.

How Much Was Fresh Money?

A large share arrived through leverage. In a typical structure, a bank's overseas branch or GIFT City unit lends an NRI nine dollars for every dollar of their own, and the full amount goes into an FCNR deposit pledged against the loan — a carry trade in which the depositor pockets the spread and the deposit pays off the loan at maturity. ICICI, which raised about $18 billion, said only about a quarter of it was plain NRI money. Across the system, loans from banks' GIFT City units alone backed close to half the haul.

That structure explains this quarter's paradox: deposits surged while net interest margins fell at every big private bank. The leveraged leg earns a thin spread — about 1% on ICICI's overseas book against over 4% at home — and dilutes margin ratios even as absolute profit grows. Public-sector bank chiefs, speaking at the Business Standard BFSI Summit, credited India's growth story and the GIFT City ecosystem for mobilising the deposits; SBI's retail operations head said the RBI's early closure of the window was a surprise.

The 2029 Question

"We don't need to panic about it today, but we must be strategic about it."

— Uday Kotak, founder, Kotak Mahindra Bank

Veteran banker Uday Kotak described the scheme as a "strong insurance policy" against global shocks, but warned that India must prepare to repay $160 billion to $170 billion, including interest, over the next three to five years, according to TradingView News. Kotak noted the closure on August 31 locked in funding before US bond yields rose sharply in early September, which would have made the same borrowing at least 100 basis points more expensive.

There is a precedent, and it ended calmly. The 2013 window's deposits matured in late 2016; the RBI had bought dollars in advance, India's FCNR pool more than halved in a single quarter, and about a quarter of the new money stayed on. This time the pile is far bigger, banks have not disclosed how much is three-year versus five-year money, and the rupees raised are now funding loans in India that do not mature on the RBI's schedule. Banks will have to replace cheap, strings-free funding with whatever deposits cost in 2029 — which is why what NRI depositors choose to roll over will matter well beyond their own returns.
